reasoning: The study generated new research data: original PET imaging (11C-PBR28 and 18F-flortaucipir) and MRI scans from patients and controls, plus new neuropathology tissue data, collected specifically for this research (data generated, used, and only available 'upon reasonable request' which still counts as generated). For software, the authors only used existing, established tools (FreeSurfer, PMOD, SPM12, SPSS, MATLAB curve-fitting toolbox) for processing/analysis without claiming to create or significantly extend any software themselves, so this is S2 (software used) rather than S1.

The paper generates research data: it conducts a large spectroscopic host-galaxy redshift survey (3147 new redshifts for PS1 SN candidates, observed with Hectospec/MMT, APO, WIYN, AAT), which is clearly newly created research data (D1). It also claims to have created research software: it implements the BEAMS method as custom code, explicitly stating "Our code is available online" with a GitHub link and example input files (footnote 19, Jones 2017), distinct from the existing packages it also uses (SNANA, emcee, CosmoMC). This custom BEAMS implementation constitutes created research software (S1), even though the paper also uses existing software/tools (SNANA simulations, emcee, CosmoMC, SExtractor, RVSAO). Per the general rule, when software/data is both generated and used, the paper is classified under the generated category, yielding S1D1.

The paper used R and standard packages (mgcv, jtrans) purely as statistical/analysis tools, not as a contribution of research software in its own right, so this is S3 (no research software). The paper generated substantial new research data: experimental tick infestation, blood sample assays (erythrocyte/leukocyte profiles, PBMC proliferation, IgG1/IgG2 ELISA responses), and PTPRC genotyping of 34 cattle, all newly collected for this study (data generated), placing it in D1.

This is a conceptual/theoretical paper that reviews literature on bureaucracy and Weber's concepts, then maps them onto the Balanced Scorecard framework. The authors explicitly state "This paper does not offer empirical support for the arguments made" - it is purely a literature-based conceptual analysis with no research data collected or analyzed, and no research software created or used.

This is a literature review paper (explicitly labeled "Review" in the journal) summarizing existing technologies and prior studies on energy storage for renewable-energy-driven water desalination systems. The authors do not create or use any research software (no simulations, models, or code attributed to this paper's own work), nor do they generate or use research data themselves—they only cite and discuss results, costs, and findings reported in other researchers' papers. Hence S3 (No Research Software) and D3 (No Research Data).

The paper uses existing research software tools (Weka and JADBio, both established ML research software/platforms) to analyze data, and also applies the SANN method from prior work rather than creating new software — so software is Used (S2), not generated. For data, while the 192-case clinical dataset was reused from a prior publication, the authors also collected new assessment data for their novel autism screening questionnaires (administered to 30 and 18 patients respectively), which constitutes newly generated research data as part of this study. Since generating data implies also using it, this falls under D1 (Data Generated).

The paper develops and implements a novel hierarchical EMS control algorithm (MILP-based high-level EM, ANFIS forecasting, and an adaptive-autoregression real-time predictive controller) as scripts/code running in MATLAB and LabVIEW specifically for this research, which constitutes research software generated (MATLAB/LabVIEW themselves are generic tools, but the control/optimization algorithms coded within them are the authors' own research software contribution). The paper also generates research data: simulation outputs (seasonal cost/SOC/forecast results for each season) and experimental measurement data collected from the laboratory microgrid (load, PV, SOC, timing data), in addition to using some existing external data (PVOutput, SODA weather, CREST-generated load profiles). Since generated software and data take precedence per the general rule, the paper is classified as S1D1.

The study generated new research data: raw ambisonic audio/360° video recordings in Peace Gardens, edited soundscape samples, and survey/questionnaire data (SQE and LoW responses from 120 participants). This counts as data generated (D1). The software mentioned (SPSS, Matlab, Adobe Audition CC) are generic statistical/processing/editing tools used as utilities for analysis and video editing, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so this falls under S3 (no research software).

The study generated new research data by collecting original behavioral observations of Palawan binturong via CCTV monitoring during zoo open/closed periods, which qualifies as D1 (data generated). No research software was created or used beyond generic statistical/utility tools (R for statistical analysis, Microsoft Excel for data entry), both of which are excluded as "generic statistical/data processing software" used merely as utilities rather than research software contributions, so this is S3.

The paper reports a post-hoc analysis of a cluster-randomised controlled trial (SSaSS) that generated new clinical trial data (fatal/non-fatal cancer events, participant records) through direct follow-up and record linkage - this counts as research data generated. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS, which is generic statistical software and explicitly excluded as research software under the criteria; there is no claim of creating or extending any research software, so this is S3."

The study uses only existing, established neuroimaging analysis tools (SPM12/DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, 3D Slicer, ICN_Atlas, SEEGA) without claiming to have created or substantially extended any software, so it is S2 (Software Used). The paper reports a new cohort of 10 patients with original EEG-fMRI acquisitions, clinical/imaging data, and DCM analysis results generated specifically for this study, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1).

This is a review article discussing existing GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on the genetic relationship between type 2 diabetes and cancer. No software was created or used in a way claimed as a research contribution (S3). The paper draws on and cites findings/statistics from previously published genetic studies and data sources (e.g., GWAS results, risk alleles, MR estimates), constituting use of existing research data rather than generation of new data (D2).

The paper develops a conceptual "agile smart lean-green" framework/model (not software) and validates it via two real-world case studies on factory shop floors (automobile and mining machinery). The authors collected original observational/fieldwork data (Gemba walk observations, brainstorming session findings, production metrics such as lead time, uptime, production rate presented in Tables 2-5) which constitutes research data generated by the research. No research software was created or used — the one mention of "design software to decide optimum path planning" is listed only as a suggested future action item, not actual software developed or employed in the study, so this is S3 (No Software). Since data was generated (and thus also used) through the case studies, this is D1.

The paper analyzes existing panel survey data (Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey, RLMS 2002-2019) using fixed-effects regressions and ordered logit models; it does not claim to create or significantly restructure a new dataset, only to use the existing RLMS data (D2). There is no claim of creating or significantly extending research software; the only software-related mention is a citation to a Stata Journal article describing a command used in the literature, not a software contribution of this paper, and statistical software use for estimation is a generic utility rather than a research software contribution (S3).

The paper is a pure linear algebra theory paper consisting of definitions, theorems, and proofs about matrix symmetry decompositions. It includes a worked numerical example (the Wilson matrix) computed by hand/by the authors to illustrate the theorems, but this is not framed as software-generated output, nor is any research software created or used as a contribution. The data availability statement explicitly says "No data was used for the research described in the article," and no research data (as defined, e.g. datasets, simulation outputs) is generated or used—only illustrative mathematical examples. Hence no software and no data: S3D3.

The paper uses a pre-existing numerical convection code (described in Willis et al. 2007, used "on request" from the corresponding author rather than developed/extended here), so software counts as Used (S2) rather than Generated. The paper runs an extensive suite of new rotating-convection simulations (68+ runs) producing simulation outputs (temperature/velocity fields, inversion-layer structures) analyzed throughout the paper—this is newly generated research data (D1), satisfying the "generated" criterion even though it's only available "on request."

The paper analyzes a pre-existing public dataset (NABEC long-read sequencing samples, accessed via AnVIL/dbGaP), so research data was used rather than generated by this study (findings/SVs are derived statistics from an existing data source). For software, the authors employed existing established tools (Sniffles2, EMBOSS/Transeq, FASTA, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram, Figtree) without claiming to create or significantly extend any new software—these are used as analysis utilities, not generated research software.

The paper uses existing data (WHO-reported laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV case counts, traveler volume/trip-length statistics, and population data) to derive estimates of severe case incidence via a mathematical formula adapted from Cauchemez et al. No new research data is generated (estimates/statistics derived from existing sources are explicitly excluded from D1), and no research software is created or used—only a formula/method and implicit generic statistical calculation, not a distinct software contribution.

The paper reports original fieldwork and laboratory histopathology: shark specimens were collected, copepod specimens dissected, and new histological sections/images were generated and analyzed, constituting generated research data (observations/measurements from fieldwork and image data). There is no mention of any research software being created or used (only generic lab equipment like a Leica autostainer), so it falls under S3 (No Research Software).

The paper isolates, sequences, and characterizes 44 new flavobacterial phage genomes (and host bacterial genomes), clearly generating novel research data (deposited at NCBI/DSMZ) — qualifying as D1. For analysis, the authors use a wide range of existing research software tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, FigTree, BLASTN, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, Geneious, ARB, RAxML, MiGA) and a previously described custom bioinformatics annotation pipeline "with modifications," but there is no clear claim within this paper of having created or significantly extended any of these software tools themselves — they are applied as existing instruments. This corresponds to S2 (software used).

The paper conducts an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study, generating synthetic data sets under various misspecification scenarios (local dependence, nonnormal latent distributions) to evaluate the LM tests — this counts as generated research data (synthetic data/simulation outputs). It also uses an existing real dataset (Miller et al., 1984) for illustration, but per the general rule, generation takes precedence over use. On the software side, the authors only rely on generic/utility tools — R's built-in "optim" function and the "NumDeriv" package for numerical derivatives — to fit models and compute test statistics; these are standard computational utilities rather than novel research software developed or substantially extended as a contribution of the paper, so this falls under S3 (no research software claimed).

The paper presents the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, an online software tool built by the research team (via contract with Anthesis group) and managed by the Cool Farm Alliance — this is clearly created research software (S1). The paper also generated new research data through structured expert elicitation (judgement and evidence scores from stakeholder workshops and expert panels across species groups/biomes), compiled into the underlying scoring tables (Supplementary Table S12) that power the metric — this is newly created/generated research data (D1), even though they also drew on existing data (Conservation Evidence database) and demonstrated the tool using a third-party farm's data. Per the general rule, generation takes precedence over use.

The paper reports original experimental research generating new research data: solid dispersions of ibuprofen with PVP and poly(2-oxazolines) were prepared and characterized via PXRD, DSC, FTIR, and dissolution studies, producing new measurements/observations (D1). No research software was created or used as a contribution — only generic instrument-associated analysis software (EVA, TA Universal Analysis, OMNIC) was used purely as utility tools for data processing/plotting, which falls under S3 per the criteria.

This is a humanities/architectural history article analyzing archival letters, exhibition catalogues, newspaper reviews, and secondary literature about Oliver Hill's 1933 Dorland Hall exhibition. No research software is created or used (no tools, code, or computational methods mentioned). The sources consulted are archival documents, letters, and literature, which fall under "Literature and Papers" — explicitly excluded from the research data definition in the criteria. No dataset is generated or used in the UKRI sense.

This is a scoping review synthesizing findings from 7 existing clinical studies on fluoride mouthwashes and orthodontic appliances. No new research data was generated; the authors extracted and summarized data from existing published studies (D2). The only software mentioned (EndNote for duplicate removal) is a widely-used generic utility tool, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so this counts as S3.

The paper reports a novel crystal structure determination, generating new research data (crystallographic structure data, CIF, CCDC deposit 1537099) through X-ray diffraction experiments. Software used (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND, SHELXTL) are existing, established crystallography tools used as utilities for data collection/structure solution/refinement/visualization; there is no claim of creating or extending software, so this is S2 (software used) combined with D1 (data generated).

The paper reports an original evaluation involving interviews and focus group discussions with 22 teachers, generating new qualitative research data (transcripts) that were analysed and reported on, placing it in D1. NVivo is mentioned only as a utility tool for coding/clustering transcripts, not as research software created, extended, or claimed as a contribution in its own right, and no other research software is used or developed, so S3 applies.

This is a review article (Frontiers in Chemistry, "Review" type) that surveys and synthesizes existing literature on protein-ionic liquid interactions. The authors did not create or use any research software themselves—mentions of simulations, MD, and COSMO-RS methodology all refer to work done in cited external studies, not computational work performed by the paper's authors. The paper does compile and tabulate existing research data (e.g., Tables 1 and 2 listing solubility values, dissolution conditions, and experimental findings drawn from the cited literature), constituting use of existing research data, but there is no claim of generating new data. Hence S3 (No Software) and D2 (Data Used).

This is a qualitative, longitudinal single-case study (Ach. Brito) based on original empirical material the authors collected themselves: 25 personal interviews, non-participant observations, and archival/documentary research conducted between 2007 and 2014. This constitutes newly generated research data (interview transcripts, field observations). There is no mention of any research software being created or used—only standard qualitative content analysis of the collected material, with no software contribution claimed.

This is an experimental physics paper reporting new room-temperature ODMR measurements on single hBN defects. The authors generate substantial new research data (PL spectra, ODMR spectra, g²(τ) correlation measurements, saturation curves) through their own experiments, satisfying D1. The "Code availability" statement only refers to generic analysis code used for fitting (exponential decays, Lorentzians) and spin-Hamiltonian simulations as a utility to interpret data; there is no claim of creating or significantly extending research software as a contribution in its own right, so this falls under S3 per the taxonomy's rule that utility-only software use is not counted as software generated or used.
